title: The BEST Workout if you like to waste time for no results (Ryan Humiston Split/PPL)
summary: Reviews Ryan Humiston's free push and pull workouts and condemns them as bro-split junk volume: isolation openers, 15-30 rep sets, sandbagging and deadlifts placed fourth. He rewrites the pull day as a 50-minute compound-led session with supersets and argues for spreading back volume across the week.
claims: Judge a fitness influencer by the programs he gives his audience rather than by drama about him
Never open a session with an isolation movement: you are freshest and strongest at the start, so use a compound
Doing cable flies at low, mid and high heights to hit every chest fiber is gimmicky wishful thinking for beginners and intermediates
Pre-fatiguing with flies so you stay weaker on presses and avoid injury is a cop-out; heavy low-rep pressing with good technique won't injure you
You need to accumulate as much tonnage as possible by pushing performance
Holding the weight at lockout for two seconds does nothing; with joints locked you are simply resting
15 reps is too high for the first compound of the day; stopping around 10 reps would be plenty
If you hit 15 reps and could get 5 more after 13 seconds of rest, you were not at failure; you stopped because of pump or other factors
The push day piles up roughly 300 chest reps, and 65-75% of them do almost nothing: junk volume
Front delts need no extra isolation after all the pressing; medial and rear delts are the ones that need the work
Doing raises front, then side, then rear with little rest leaves nothing in the tank for the rear delts
20-rep sets sit outside a relevant intensity window; 3x6-10 dumbbell shoulder press is lighter in total tonnage but more productive than 180 reps of raises
10 sets of 20 reps of triceps cable work is a waste of time
Choosing exercises by what hurts most leads to moves that don't fit your anthropometry and to chasing the pump
An obsession with mind-muscle connection keeps the muscle small when it produces piles of useless reps
The push session takes about two hours; a compound-led session with supersets would take about 1h10 and give better gains
Bro splits build the day around one muscle instead of compounds, which is why they fail; he gives the push day 0/20
The majority of a program's tonnage must come from compounds: they give high intensity ratios and save time
Two warm-up sets of 30 reps are useless
Order exercises by priority, with the ones giving the most tonnage first
Doing 4x15 with no drop in reps across sets is sandbagging; use an evolving rep range like 12-15 or 10-15
With huge volume you have to sandbag early sets just to get through, which turns lifting into cardio with weights
Open back day with a leg movement, or with a heavy row, Pendlay row or heavy weighted pull-up
The upper back can take a lot of volume, but 15-20 reps on every exercise is wasted quality
With 6 reps to failure even the first rep is close to failure; with 100 reps the first 80 are nowhere near it
Artificial failure (pump, breathing) feels great but builds nothing; organic failure, where the fibers can't produce force anymore, is what grows muscle
Never deadlift as your fourth exercise; open the day with it
Deadlift 5-7 reps max, 5 is enough, for 1-3 sets; for hamstring and glute volume use another hip hinge for 3x6-10 or 3x8-12
10-rep deadlift sets are too much for novices and 30 reps is absurd: people fail on cardio, not muscle
High reps wreck progression math: adding 5 lb to a 30-rep set adds 150 lb of tonnage, while a single set of 5 is easy to progress
A finisher only makes sense after real work has used up the muscle; as the first biceps work it is just junk volume
His 50-minute pull day: deadlift 1-3x2-5; dumbbell rows 3x8-12 superset curls 3x8-12; weighted chins or pull-ups 4x3-5 or 4x5-7 superset biceps or forearm isolation 4x8-12
Spread back volume through the week: rather than 30 sets once, do about 6 sets on each training day
Train legs on back day; for example superset an RDL or paused squat with chin-ups
Warm-up sets do count, because they fatigue you
Long, repetitive programs mostly create mental fatigue; people get mediocre results for two months and quit
Unilateral back work doubles training time; better to learn to pull with the back bilaterally, and pull-ups beat unilateral lat moves
Keeping a slightly bent arm helps keep the back engaged; he agrees with Humiston on this
Waddling with back pain after deadlifts comes from bad technique or too many reps, not from opening the day with deadlifts
Enhanced lifters can train however they want; naturals should avoid this kind of program
